content.text: I drafted all four explanations and cited only aliases from each rule's own allowed list. For Jersey City, I kept the amendment's "or otherwise utilize" wording and the Service Provider definition, and left out the adoption and approval dates. For California, I explained subsection (b) coercion and flagged subsection (a) as a separate conspiracy prohibition. For New Jersey, I attributed only the two positive statements (credit report cost and reasonable application fees) and treated employment verification as a request. For Hoboken, I included the fine since the text states it, and left out all dates.

claims.text: In Jersey City, it is unlawful for a real estate lessor, an agent, or a subcontractor of either to subscribe to, contract with, exchange anything of value for, or otherwise use the services of a "Service Provider." A Service Provider is any person who performs a "coordination" function for a lessor. Coordination means collecting nonpublic competitor information from lessors (plus historical or current prices, supply levels, occupancy rates, or lease termination and renewal dates from two or more lessors or from public databases), processing it with a system or software that uses computation, and recommending rents, lease terms, or occupancy levels to a lessor. The definition does not cover owners of multiple properties acting only on properties controlled by the same owner, and it does not cover licensed real estate agents who are operating in accordance with applicable state regulations. The rules also apply only to "residential dwelling units," meaning units intended as a person's primary residence, and they exclude inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care, and detention or correctional facilities. A separate provision says no service provider may facilitate an agreement not to compete among lessors on rental pricing, fees, or other rental terms.

Under California's new Business and Professions Code section 16729, subsection (b) makes it unlawful for a person to use or distribute a "common pricing algorithm" if that person coerces another person to set or adopt a price or commercial term the algorithm recommends for the same or similar products or services in California. A common pricing algorithm is any methodology, including a computer, software, or other technology, used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend, align, stabilize, set, or otherwise influence a price or commercial term. "Distribute" includes selling, licensing, providing access to, or otherwise making available, including by subscription. A "person" does not include the end consumer of a product or service. Coercion is not the only way to violate the section. Subsection (a) separately makes it unlawful to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade. This is a general rule about common pricing algorithms, not a rental-specific ban.

New Jersey's Truth in Renting guide, in its credit and background check passage, says a landlord is allowed to charge a prospective tenant for the cost of the credit report. It also says the landlord may request reasonable rental application fees or employment verification. Employment verification is described as something the landlord may request, not as a fee. These are the only fee statements the passage makes, and it does not address anything beyond them.

In Hoboken, a residential landlord who wants to raise a current tenant's rent by more than 10% year over year when renewing the lease must make four disclosures to the tenant before the increase is implemented. The disclosures go either in the renewal lease, clearly indicated on its first page, or on a form provided by the Hoboken Division of Housing. They are: (1) an itemization of the costs associated with the increase; (2) a statement whether a rent algorithm was used to set it; (3) a statement that the tenant may take legal action, at their own expense, if they believe the increase is unconscionable or otherwise not in accordance with local or state law; and (4) the Division of Housing's contact information, with a statement that tenants may reach out to the Division and/or the Tenant Advocate with questions or concerns. A landlord who pleads guilty to or is found guilty of failing to provide these disclosures can be fined up to $1,000 per incident. This rule is about disclosures for increases over 10%, not a cap on rent increases.
